title: Agnaye svāhā: the vaiśvadeva and the bali offerings
theme: The formulas of the household’s daily offering from the cooked food: oblations into the fire to Agni, the gods and the firm ones, and portions set down for dharma, the waters, the house, the boundaries, all beings, the fathers, people and the spirits who roam, with a prayer for undiminished grain.

words.role: recipient; the anonymous commentator counts dhruva among the well-known deities

words.meaning: to bhūma — the earth, or the abundant one (not explained by the commentator)
to him whose abode is firm
words.context: the anonymous commentator: «ध्रुवा क्षितिरवस्थितिर्यस्य सोऽयं ध्रुवक्षितिः»

words.meaning: to him whose abode does not fall

words.context: the anonymous commentator: «कदाचित्प्रमादालस्यादिना दुरिष्टमपि कर्म स्विष्टं करोतीति स्विष्टकृत्» — he makes well offered even a rite ill offered through carelessness or sloth

words.meaning: to the plants and the trees

sandhi.type: visarga before a voiced consonant; visarga before s
sandhi.rule: viśvebhyaḥ + devebhyaḥ → viśvebhyo devebhyaḥ; devebhyaḥ + svāhā → devebhyas svāhā (the recitation doubles the s).

samasa.meaning: he whose abode does not fall
he who makes [the rite] well offered

morphology.note: Dative of an a-stem bhūma; the classical word is bhūman (‘earth’, or ‘abundance’). The anonymous commentator does not explain it.
Dative plural of ap, ‘water’, which is used in the plural; the p becomes d before bh.

translation.literal: To Agni svāhā. To all the gods svāhā. To the firm one, to bhūma svāhā. To the one of firm abode svāhā. To the one of unfailing abode svāhā. To Agni the maker of the well-offered svāhā. To dharma svāhā. To adharma svāhā. To the waters svāhā. To the plants and trees svāhā.
translation.readable: To Agni, svāhā; to all the gods, svāhā; to the Firm, to the Earth, svāhā; to the One whose abode is firm, svāhā; to the One whose abode does not fail, svāhā; to Agni who makes the offering whole, svāhā; to right conduct, svāhā; to its opposite, svāhā; to the waters, svāhā; to the plants and the trees, svāhā.

words.meaning: to the rakṣases and the attendants of the gods
words.context: the anonymous commentator: «रक्षांसि च देवजनाश्च रक्षोदेवजनाः»; the devajanas are «देवानां भृत्यवर्गाः», the gods’ servants
the anonymous commentator: «गृहे विद्यमाना गृह्याः कुलदेवताः» — the family deities present in the house
the anonymous commentator: the deities at the edges of the house

words.meaning: to the lords of the boundaries

words.context: the anonymous commentator: the lord of Rati, who bewilders the three worlds
the anonymous commentator: here, the wind that dwells in the mid-region
the anonymous commentator: «वैदिकशब्दराशिवाचकेन नामशब्देन तद्वेद्यः परमात्मा लक्ष्यते» — the Name, the whole of the Vedic word, points to the supreme self it makes known
the anonymous commentator: here, the deity who presides over the middle world

sandhi.type: visarga before s; -as as -o in the compound

sandhi.rule: yat + ejati → yad ejati: t is voiced before a vowel.
yat + ca → yac ca: t assimilates to c.

sandhi.type: visarga before a voiced consonant; -aḥ before a
sandhi.rule: nāmnaḥ + bhāgaḥ → nāmno bhāgaḥ; bhāgaḥ + ayam → bhāgo ’yam.

samasa.meaning: the rakṣases and the gods’ attendants; devajana is itself a ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa, देवानां जनाः, the gods’ people

morphology.note: Dative plural of the feminine gṛhyā, ‘belonging to the house’, with devatā understood (the commentator: «कुलदेवताः»).

Genitive of nāman, ‘name’; with nāmne (dative) the line plays on the one word. The anonymous commentator takes the Name as the supreme self, whose portion is all that moves, to be taken back at the dissolution.

translation.literal: To the rakṣases and the gods’ attendants svāhā. To the [deities] of the house svāhā. To the boundaries svāhā. To the lords of the boundaries svāhā. To all beings svāhā. To Kāma svāhā. To the mid-region svāhā. What stirs in the world and what moves — this is the portion of the Name; to the Name svāhā. To the earth svāhā. To the mid-region svāhā.
translation.readable: To the rakṣases and the attendants of the gods, svāhā; to the deities of the house, svāhā; to the boundaries and to their lords, svāhā; to all beings, svāhā; to Desire, svāhā; to the mid-region, svāhā. Whatever in the world stirs, whatever moves, is the share of the Name: to the Name, svāhā. To the earth, svāhā; to the mid-region, svāhā.

words.context: the anonymous commentator: Virāj
the anonymous commentator: Hiraṇyagarbha

words.meaning: svadhā, the call of offering to the fathers

words.context: the anonymous commentator: the Agniṣvātta and other fathers
the anonymous commentator: «ब्रह्मादिस्थावरान्ताधिपतये» — the lord of all, from Brahmā to the motionless

morphology.note: Dative of the s-stem candramas, ‘the moon’.
The call used in offerings to the fathers, as svāhā is to the gods; here both are said.

translation.literal: To the sky svāhā. To the sun svāhā. To the moon svāhā. To the constellations svāhā. To Indra svāhā. To Bṛhaspati svāhā. To Prajāpati svāhā. To Brahmā svāhā. Svadhā to the fathers, svāhā. Homage to Rudra, the lord of creatures, svāhā.
translation.readable: To the sky, the sun, the moon and the stars, svāhā; to Indra, to Bṛhaspati, to Prajāpati, to Brahmā, svāhā. To the fathers, svadhā and svāhā. Homage to Rudra, lord of all creatures, svāhā.

words.context: the anonymous commentator: Indra and the rest
the anonymous commentator: a class of deities («देवविशेषेभ्यो»)

words.meaning: hanta, the call with which food is given to people
to the one who stands highest
words.context: the anonymous commentator: «परमेष्ठी चतुर्मुखो ब्रह्मा» — Brahmā of the four faces
the anonymous commentator: «कूप उदकाधारविशेषः» — a kind of reservoir of water
the anonymous commentator glosses «एवैवं» — so, thus

words.meaning: to Dhanadhānī, she who holds wealth
words.context: the anonymous commentator: «धनानि दधाति पोषयति भक्तानामिति धनधानी काचिद्देवता» — a goddess who holds and nourishes the wealth of her devotees
the anonymous commentator: «ये भूता ग्रहविशेषा» — a kind of seizing spirits

words.meaning: an offering, a share of food
of Vituda, the one who strikes

words.context: the anonymous commentator: «प्रेष्याः प्रेषणीया भृत्या इति यावत्» — servants
the anonymous commentator: «तेभ्यो बलिं हरामि भूमौ निक्षिपामि» — I set the offering down on the ground

sandhi.rule: pitṛbhyaḥ + svadhā → pitṛbhyas svadhā; svadhā + astu → svadhā ’stu, ā and a fusing into ā.
sahasradhāram + akṣitam: the m is joined to the vowel.

sandhi.type: visarga after i before a voiced consonant

sandhi_exceptions.note: सहस्रधारो अक्षितः: the visarga of sahasradhāraḥ becomes o before a and the a is kept, not elided; the witnesses write it so (a Vedic usage).
मे अस्तु: the e of the enclitic me is kept before a, without the elision of the a that classical sandhi would make; as the witnesses write it.

morphology.note: The interjection hanta, the call with which food is given to people, written in the base with a long final ā. The anonymous commentator names the four calls svāhā, svadhā, namaḥ and hanta as the particles with which food is given to gods, fathers, beings and people.
Vedic form of eva/evam, ‘so’, with a long final ā.
Masculine plural of bhūta (classically neuter), ‘beings’; the commentator takes them as a kind of spirits.

Genitive of vituda, from vi-√tud, ‘to strike, pierce’. The anonymous commentator: «विशेषेण तुदति पापिनः प्राणिनः पीडयतीति वितुदः» — he who strikes especially the wrongdoers; for him, Rudra as the fire of time, who dwells in the cremation ground. This is the commentator’s reading.

translation.literal: To the gods svāhā. To the fathers let there be svadhā. To beings homage. To men hanta. To Prajāpati svāhā. To Parameṣṭhin svāhā. As a well of a hundred streams, of a thousand streams, [is] undiminished, so let grain be for me, of a thousand streams, undiminished. To Dhanadhānī svāhā. The beings who roam by day and night wanting an offering, the servants of Vituda — to them I, desiring increase, bring an offering; may the lord of increase place increase in me. Svāhā.
translation.readable: To the gods, svāhā; to the fathers, svadhā; to all beings, homage; to people, hanta. To Prajāpati and to the One who stands highest, svāhā. As a well with a hundred, a thousand streams never runs dry, so may my grain be — a thousand streams, never running dry. To the goddess who holds wealth, svāhā. To the beings who roam by day and by night wanting an offering, the servants of the Striker, I set out this offering, wishing for increase: may the lord of increase place increase in me. Svāhā.

syntax: Almost every line is a dative of the recipient followed by a call of offering (svāhā, svadhā, namaḥ, hanta), with no verb. Two sentences are full: the relative clause yad ejati … ceṣṭati with nāmno bhāgo ’yam (86), and the comparison yathā kūpaḥ … evā me astu dhānyam (88). The last formula is a relative clause (ye bhūtāḥ … preṣyāḥ) taken up by tebhyaḥ, the verb harāmi and a wish in the imperative (dadhātu).

ambiguities.note: Unit 86 has ‘to the mid-region’ twice. The anonymous commentator separates them: the first means the wind that dwells in the mid-region, the second the deity who presides over the middle world.

nāmno bhāgo ’yam nāmne svāhā: the anonymous commentator takes ‘Name’ as the whole of the Vedic word, and so the supreme self it makes known, whose portion everything that moves is, to be taken back at the dissolution. The text itself does not explain the word.
dhruvāya bhūmāya: the commentator names dhruva as a well-known deity but does not explain bhūma; ‘the earth’ and ‘the abundant one’ are both possible.

metre.name: mixed
metre.note: The offering formulas are prose. yathā kūpaḥ … akṣitam is a couplet in anuṣṭubh rhythm, of 16 and 15 syllables as written (me astu keeps its hiatus). ye bhūtāḥ … preṣyāḥ (22 syllables) and tebhyo baliṃ … dadhātu (22, then svāhā) are each two triṣṭubh lines of 11.

beginner: This anuvāka gives the words for an old household rite done every day with the cooked food. First small portions are offered into the fire, each with ‘svāhā’: to Agni, to all the gods, to the firm and lasting ones, and to Agni who makes the offering whole. Then portions are set down on the ground for many others: right conduct and its opposite, the waters and plants, the deities of the house and its boundaries, all beings, the sky, sun, moon and stars, the great gods, the ancestors, and people. Each kind of recipient has its own call: svāhā for gods, svadhā for ancestors, namaḥ for beings, hanta for people. The prayer that grain be like a well that never runs dry, and the last offering to the spirits who roam, end it. The edition reports the rite as the commentator describes it.
analogy: Like a host who, before eating, sets aside a portion for every guest in the house, the neighbours and the stranger at the door.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It names, one by one, the recipients of the household’s daily offering: Agni, all the gods, the firm and unfailing ones, Agni the maker of the well-offered; dharma and adharma, the waters, plants and trees, rakṣases and the gods’ attendants, the deities of the house and its boundaries, all beings, Kāma, the mid-region, the Name, earth, sky, sun, moon and stars, Indra, Bṛhaspati, Prajāpati, Brahmā, the fathers, Rudra, the gods, beings, people, Parameṣṭhin and Dhanadhānī; it asks for grain like an inexhaustible well, and sets out a share for the spirits who roam.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: the first formulas are «इतः परं वैश्वदेवकर्मणि विनियुक्ताः षड्ढोममन्त्रा व्याख्यायन्ते» — the six formulas of oblation used in the vaiśvadeva rite; from dharmāya on: «इतः परं बलिहरणकर्मणि विनियुक्ता मन्त्रा व्याख्यायन्ते» — the formulas used in setting out the bali offerings. Of the Name he says the offering is given on the ground («बलिहरणरूपमिदं हविर्भूमौ दत्तमस्तु»).

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: food is to be given to gods, fathers, beings and people with the four particles svāhā, svadhā, namaḥ and hanta; said with these words, the gift pleases them more, as kind words do with a meal. He adds that svāhā may be supplied with namaḥ for the beings, or namaḥ itself taken as the word of giving food.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: «कदाचित्प्रमादालस्यादिना दुरिष्टमपि कर्म स्विष्टं करोतीति स्विष्टकृत्» — the one who makes well offered even what was ill offered through carelessness or sloth.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: as a well, «कूप उदकाधारविशेषः», with many streams stays undiminished however much water is drawn from it, so by the favour of the supreme self may my grain be inexhaustible, and filled in many granaries. The offering then goes to a goddess he calls Dhanadhānī: «धनानि दधाति पोषयति भक्तानामिति धनधानी काचिद्देवता».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: «तेभ्यो बलिं हरामि भूमौ निक्षिपामि» — I set the offering on the ground for them, wishing for increase. They are a kind of seizing spirits, servants of Vituda, whom he identifies as Rudra in the form of the fire of time, dwelling in the cremation ground, who strikes the wrongdoers. These identifications are his.

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this text is in the edition’s sources: Raṅgarāmānuja’s is not available, and the commentaries present (the anonymous bhāṣya, Sāyaṇa, Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara) are ritual and Vedic explanations, not school readings. Only the anonymous commentator explains this anuvāka; Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara have no comment on it in the edition’s sources.

parallels.note: The Gītā speaks of those who eat what remains of the sacrifice; the vaiśvadeva and bali offerings are made from the cooked food before the household eats.

contemporary.text: Before the household eats, the rite sets aside a share for a long list of others: the gods, the ancestors, the plants and waters, the house and its edges, all beings, people, even the spirits that roam. Whatever one makes of the recipients, the habit of thinking first of who else a meal depends on, and who else is hungry, is widely shared. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Why might a household set aside a share of food before eating it?
reflect.deeper: The rite gives a different call to gods, ancestors, beings and people. What does it suggest that each relation is addressed differently?
reflect.practice: Before a meal, think for a moment of the people and things it depended on.

references.text: Only the anonymous commentary explains this anuvāka; Sāyaṇa’s and Bhāskara’s commentaries in the edition’s sources do not.

flags.note: The edition’s computed map gives Bhāskara 2 for 10.67; his anuvāka 2 is not on these formulas, and he has no comment on this anuvāka.
हन्ता is analysed as the interjection hanta (the commentator’s hantakāra), written long in the base.
Two Vedic hiatuses in unit 88 (सहस्रधारो अक्षितः, मे अस्तु) are declared as the witnesses write them.
